data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Reduced evapotranspiration in cities is the dominant nocturnal UHI mechanism; the cross-city gap is largest where urban vegetation and irrigation are scarcest, because the absence of latent heat loss forces all energy into sensible heating of the air.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If heavily irrigated, vegetated cities still exhibit a large nocturnal UHI, the evapotranspiration mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI persists strongly during periods when evapotranspiration is negligible (e.g., after rainfall, in winter), the mechanism is weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If cities with high vegetation cover show no reduction in the nocturnal gap compared to barren cities, the mechanism is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Vegetated countryside stays cool at night because daytime evapotranspiration removes latent heat, leaving little sensible heat to release after sunset. Cities, lacking vegetation and irrigation, partition incoming energy almost entirely into sensible heat, which warms the air directly. Cities with less green space and more impervious area therefore exhibit a larger nocturnal temperature gap.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
